newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Sandinistas demand Managua vote be annulled.
newsitem.headline: Sandinistas demand Managua vote be annulled.

text.p: Nicaragua's left-wing Sandinista Front late on Thursday called on election authorities to annul the elections held in the province of Managua due to multiple irregularities and to hold a new vote.

"Since it is impossible to determine the will of the voters in more than 50 percent of voting stations ... I ask the Supreme Election Council to declare the election null and call new elections in this province," Emmett Lang Salmeron, Sandinista legal representative in Managua, told a news conference.

The Sandinista call for the annulation of all elections held in Managua, including the presidential vote, is the latest blow to Nicaragua's October 20 elections, which have been plagued by allegations of irregularities and fraud.
Seven small political parties have also called for annulation of the vote in Managua, Nicaragua's most populous province.
The bitter post-election spat over the validity of the vote and allegations of fraud have marred what was to be an historic step in Nicaragua's conversion to democracy after years of dictatorship.
In the presidential race, former Managua Mayor Arnoldo Aleman leads former Sandinista President Daniel Ortega 49 to 38 percent with more than 87 percent of the votes counted.
While Aleman has already proclaimed himself president-elect, Ortega has refused to concede defeat, saying the vote count was riddled with irregularities and hinting at fraud by his Liberal rivals.
At the Sandinista's request, the CSE is reviewing the vote count and has said official results will not be known till mid-November.

Lang said a Sandinista review of the voting process in Managua showed the vote count in 63 percent of the voting stations had serious "inconsistencies," including missing or incomplete tally sheets, and numerical inconsistencies.
He said of Managua's 2,267 voting stations, vote results were completely absent in 300 and authorities could not identify the location of 150 stations on its records.
He said 150 bags of election material labelled "unidentified" were found in the Managua vote-counting centre and many ballots were found in the streets or in garbage cans.
While refusing to specifically accuse their Liberal rivals of fraud, Lang said they had found "many fraudulent elements" in the vote.
"As Nicaraguans we have the obligation to try to save these elections and see in what circumstances, in spite of what we know, we can obtain results," he said.
If the CSE heeds the Sandinista call, it would be another major delay in a troubled vote in which official winners have still not been announced 11 days after the event.
The long delay has led to fears of political instability as angry Sandinista and Liberal Alliance activists sling fraud charges and hold wild, premature victory celebrations.
President Violeta Chamorro has issued public calls for calm and the National Police have banned public demonstrations to prevent bloodshed.
The most dangerous flashpoint is in Managua, where both the Liberal and Sandinista candidates have declared victory, putting them on a head-on collision course.

Sandinista mayoral candidate Carlos Guadamuz said a private Sandinista count showed he was the winner and called on his supporters to defend his win over Liberal Roberto Cedeno, ahead in the official count, to the "ultimate consequences."
A police report warned of a growing wave of politically motivated violence as Sandinista and Liberal Alliance activists have engaged in a series of brawls and one murder was reported.
